extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and newsroom staff producing news stories
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide giving vocabulary, capitalization, pronunciation and usage guidance to help reporters and editors write about religion, race, ethnicity, disability, immigration and other identity-related topics respectfully and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid casual use of 'gypsy' and 'gyp'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid casual use such as “they lived like gypsies, traveling from place to place” and the pejorative term gyp, (e.g. “I got gypped,”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are likely derived from Gypsy and perpetuate a negative stereotype of Roma people as swindlers and thieves. Do not use casually.

rubrics_metrics.name: hadith — pronunciation and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “ha-DEETH.” A report or reports about a saying, action or tradition of Muhammad and his closest companions. Can be used as both a singular and a plural noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadith are viewed by Muslims as explanations of the Quran and are second only to Islam’s holy book in guidance and as a source of Shariah. The two most reliable collections are by Bukhari and Muslim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing Black/African American hair — ask what style
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a person’s hair in news stories, ask what style the hair is; don't assume. Black hair comes in a variety of styles and textures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic assumptions; if relevant to the story, identify the specific style (afro, braids, cornrows, dreadlocks, extensions, Jheri curl, twists, weave, bald/shaved distinctions). Use hair descriptions to open conversations and provide context when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define specific Black hair styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear definitions for terms like afro, bald vs shaved, braids (plaits), cornrows, dreadlocks/locks, extensions, Jheri curl, twists, weave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed definitions (e.g., afro = tight curls in full rounded shape; braids = sections of three or more strands intertwined; Jheri curl = chemically treated curly hair) to label styles accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: hajj — pronunciation, significance and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “hahj.” In Islam, a pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth of the Five Pillars. Takes place during the 12th month of the Islamic year; dates move each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word is typically not capitalized. A hajji is a person who has undertaken the pilgrimage. Note associated festival (Eid al-Adha) at the end of hajj.

rubrics_metrics.name: halakhah — pronunciation and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “ha-la-KHAH.” Jewish law, the set of rules and practices governing many aspects of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by Jewish scripture and teachings; interpreted by rabbis for each generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: halal — meaning and prohibited items
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arabic, something that is lawful and permitted in Islam; refers to foods, objects and activities sanctioned by Islamic teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halal slaughter requires invoking God's name and cutting the throat to drain blood. Pork, blood, intoxicants and alcohol are not halal; forbidden objects and activities are called haram.

rubrics_metrics.name: hamesh/hamsa — correct terms and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamesh is the Hebrew word for hamsa (Arabic); means five or 'five fingers of the hand.' Hamsa is a palm-shaped symbol worn for good luck or protection that predates Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cross-cultural use (Latin American, Greek, Ethiopian, Turkish) and that some Muslims call it 'hand of Fatima.' Note that hamsa is often non-religious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'handicapped' when describing people
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not describe a person as handicapped unless it is central to the story; avoid using handicap and handicapped when describing a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the specific condition. The term may still be used when citing laws/regulations or places (e.g., handicapped parking), though many prefer 'accessible parking.' Use person-first language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanukkah — preferred spelling and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jewish Festival of Lights; preferred spelling Hanukkah, though Chanukah is also commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize Hanukkah. To find dates, consult Jewish holidays resources such as Hebcal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hapa — origin and contemporary usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally from Hawaiian 'hapa haole' meaning 'half white/foreigner'; once considered derogatory, now often a positive self-identifier for people of mixed white and other ancestry, especially Asians and Pacific Islanders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of history and current embrace as self-identification by many.

rubrics_metrics.name: haraam vs haram — distinguish meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: haraam (pronounced 'ha-RAHM') means something forbidden in Islam; haram (pronounced 'HAR-em') refers to a sanctuary or sacred territory considered inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct term and pronunciation according to intended meaning (forbidden vs sanctuary).

rubrics_metrics.name: hard of hearing — acceptable usage and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Term may be used for people with mild to moderate hearing loss who usually use speech to communicate; 'Hard of hearing' is almost always acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some may prefer 'Deaf' or 'deaf' depending on cultural affiliation. Prefer the term the person uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haredi/Haredim — usage and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebrew term meaning 'fear' or 'anxiety' applied to devout believers; Haredim plural can be used for strictly observant Orthodox Jews instead of 'ultra-Orthodox.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the term is not widely used outside Israel and Jewish media; use cautiously and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: HaShem — usage in place of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Word some Jews use instead of saying 'God'; literally means 'The Name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use HaShem appropriately as a reverent substitute in Jewish contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasidism/Hasidic — definition and adjectival form
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasidism is a social and religious movement stressing devotion and reverence to a rebbe; followers are Hasidim and the adjectival form is Hasidic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these terms accurately to describe the movement and its adherents.

rubrics_metrics.name: hate crime — use FBI definition and context
rubrics_metrics.description: FBI: a traditional offense (murder, arson, vandalism) with an added element of bias; Congress defines hate crime as a criminal offense motivated in whole or in part by bias against protected characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note hate itself is not a crime; be mindful of freedom of speech and civil liberties when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hawaiian — ethnic identifier, not residence descriptor
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: Hawaiian refers to an ethnic group of Polynesian descent and should not be used for everyone living in Hawaii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternatives like 'Hawaiʻi resident' when referring to people who live in Hawaii but are not ethnically Hawaiian. See Pacific Islander.

rubrics_metrics.name: HBCU — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically Black colleges and universities, established before 1964 to provide educational opportunities to people of African descent; about 100 exist in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HBCU is acceptable on second reference and in headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'hearing impaired' — prefer person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms 'hearing impaired' and 'hearing impairment' describe a range of hearing loss but are disliked as they describe a person by a deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Federation of the Deaf finds 'hearing impaired' unacceptable; use 'deaf' for total hearing loss or 'partial hearing loss' and prefer asking the person's preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: henna and mehndi — correct usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Henna is a plant used to make ink or hair dye; ceremonial application designs on hands/feet are called mehndi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe cultural practices accurately (e.g., Indian women wear mehndi for weddings) and note designs fade after about a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'hermaphrodite' — prefer 'intersex'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hermaphrodite is derogatory when referring to intersex individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'intersex' and avoid hermaphrodite.

rubrics_metrics.name: heteronormative/heteronormativity — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the assumption that heterosexuality is the norm, which marginalizes queer people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the terms to describe cultural assumptions and structures that privilege heterosexuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: heterosexism — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude that heterosexuality is the only valid sexual orientation, often expressed by ignoring LGBTQ people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately to describe attitudes or institutional norms; give examples (e.g., Valentine’s Day coverage that omits same-sex couples).

rubrics_metrics.name: heterosexual — restricted usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective describing people attracted to the opposite sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'heterosexual' primarily in medical contexts or when referencing sexual activity; for general usage prefer 'straight' or other context-appropriate terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Holy Days — definition and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: The 10-day period beginning with Rosh Hashanah and ending with Yom Kippur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize and consult holiday calendars (Hebcal) for dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: hijab — definition and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally describes the scarf many Muslim women use to cover their head; can also refer to modest dress in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize regional, sectarian and personal variation (Shiites more likely to wear; family members may differ). Women decide based on mosque, community and conscience. Be sensitive to differing views of veiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindi vs Hindu — do not confuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindi is a primary language of India; do not confuse Hindi (language) with Hindu (religious designation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct term and refer to Hindu for religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindu, Hinduism — definition and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinduism (Sanatana Dharma) is an ancient religious/spiritual system with diverse practices; capitalize 'guru' before a name on first reference and use last name thereafter; 'Swami' as a title should be capitalized before a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe beliefs (karma, rebirth) and diversity of practice; use titles and capitalization correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindustan/Hindustani — cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindustan once referred to a northern Indian empire but is sometimes used for the Indian subcontinent; Hindustani is an unofficial language (mix of Urdu and Hindi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with Hindustan's broad usage and colonial connotations; see references for Indian languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: hip-hop — broader cultural movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Hip-hop includes deejaying, MCing/emceeing/rapping, graffiti painting and breakdancing; goes well beyond music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hip-hop' (or 'hip hop') and recognize the four elements and cultural origins in the South Bronx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispanic — definition, ethnicity vs race, and regional preference
rubrics_metrics.description: An umbrella term for people of Spanish-speaking origin; federal policy defines Hispanic as an ethnicity, not a race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize regional preference differences (term more common in Eastern U.S. and Caribbean/South American ancestry); consult resources and research on preferences; U.S. Census uses 'Hispanic or Latino.' See related entries (Latino, Latina, Latinx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispanic paradox — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies showing Hispanic communities may have longer life expectancy despite higher risk factors for illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use term when reporting on relevant epidemiological findings and cite studies attributing causes like family cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispaniola — geographic clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Large Caribbean island containing the Dominican Republic (east) and Haiti (west).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geographic name accurately and note the meaning 'Isle of Spain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hmong — ethnic group definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethnic group living in southern China, Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand; many resettled in the U.S. after the Laotian civil war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe origins and migration history appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hmong names — naming order
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name second; one-syllable names are often common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect naming order and conventions when reporting names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holocaust — capitalization and contextual sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize when referring to the murder of six million Jews and others during World War II; lowercase in other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to the term's association with genocide; note alternative term Shoʾah is preferred in Israel and France. Avoid casual use of 'holocaust' for unrelated events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy See — distinct entity from Vatican City
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of reverence for the Diocese of Rome referring to the pope and his Curia when official church actions are taken; distinct from the Vatican city-state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Holy See' when referring to the papal administrative entity and consult Vatican sources for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Spirit — preferred modern term
rubrics_metrics.description: The third entity of the Christian Trinity, now preferred over the older term 'Holy Ghost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Holy Spirit' as the preferred term in reporting and religious contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Thursday and Holy Week — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy Thursday (Maundy Thursday) commemorates the Last Supper; Holy Week runs from Palm Sunday to Easter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard names and note denominational variations (e.g., Roman Catholic 'Passion Week').

rubrics_metrics.name: homeless — person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who lacks a fixed, regular and adequate nighttime residence; some prefer 'unhoused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible ask preference; use 'people experiencing homelessness' and avoid labels like 'the homeless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'homo' — avoid pejorative usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Homo is a pejorative term for homosexual; use only if there is a compelling reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid casual/pejorative use; prefer respectful terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: homophobia — definition and restricted usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear, hatred or dislike of homosexuality, gay men and lesbians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict use to germane contexts (quotations or analysis). Prefer 'LGBT-rights opponents' instead of labeling people as homophobes when describing opponents of LGBT rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: homosexual — restricted usage
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun or adjective describing attraction to same sex; recommended for medical contexts or reference to sexual activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general identity use 'gay' or 'lesbian' as appropriate; use 'homosexual' mainly in clinical/legal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hong Kong — political and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Former British colony, became special administrative region of China in 1997 under 'One Country, Two Systems'; ongoing tensions over meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe status accurately and note current political tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: hujjaj — plural for hajji
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers on a hajj pilgrimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term correctly as plural of hajji when referring to pilgrims.

rubrics_metrics.name: humanist — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A rationalist who believes humanity is capable of morality and self-fulfillment without supernaturalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term to describe secular ethical positions accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: husband — acceptable term with preference check
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable term for a male, legally married partner of a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask which term the subject prefers if possible; see also partner/lover.

rubrics_metrics.name: hysteria — historical roots and pejorative nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Term historically used (linked to uterus) to describe frenzied or overly emotional states, often targeting women; now pejorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution or avoid; note medical/psychiatric classification changes and past mistreatment tied to the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'identifies as' for trans people's gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the phrase 'identifies as' to write about a trans person’s gender when 'is' does not change meaning; this language questions a trans person’s gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'is' rather than 'identifies as.' Only acceptable to use 'identifies as' when quoting a trans source.

rubrics_metrics.name: idol vs murti — avoid religiously insensitive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious using 'idol' because it can imply a false god; Hindus use 'murti' for worship representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'idol' for Hindu worship objects; use 'murti' and avoid 'idol worship.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'illegal alien' — prefer alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'illegal alien' and similar terms; alternatives include 'undocumented worker' or 'undocumented immigrant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like 'illegal' criminalize the person rather than the act; never use 'illegal(s)' as a noun. Note federal agencies and immigrant-rights groups advise against the term. See USCIS memo (Feb 2021) advising use of 'noncitizen' or 'undocumented noncitizen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'illegal immigrant/illegal(s)' variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'illegal immigrant,' 'illegal alien,' 'illegals' when referring to immigration status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'undocumented immigrant' or 'undocumented worker.' Discuss undocumented status between source, reporter and editors because of deportation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: imam — pronunciation and capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'ee-MAHM.' Any person who leads congregational prayer; in formal sense a religious or political leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On first reference, capitalize 'Imam' when preceding a proper name; on second reference use only the person's last name. Uppercase 'Imam' when referencing the Twelve Imams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on immigrants — relevance and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioning a person's immigrant status or first-generation status should be relevant to the story; undocumented status presents risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss undocumented status with sources and editors because of deportation risk; avoid gratuitous identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: implicit/unconscious bias — definition and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes that unconsciously affect people’s decisions and actions; often unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize implicit bias is harmful and take steps to interrupt it by adding steps to decision-making processes and explicitly considering racial impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: independent living — definition for older adults
rubrics_metrics.description: Housing arrangement for those 55+ who can live with little or no assistance; may include apartment-style living and amenities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term accurately to describe senior housing options and characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian Country — legal term
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal term in Title 18 of the U.S. Code defining federal and tribal jurisdiction in crimes affecting Indians on reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Indian Country' accurately in legal and jurisdictional contexts; it also has popular usage describing reservations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian languages — diversity and counts
rubrics_metrics.description: India has 14 officially recognized languages and many more developed languages; in 2001 census 29 languages had 1M+ native speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these are distinct languages, not mere dialects; avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian/Indian American vs American Indian — correct usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Indian' or 'person from India' for ancestral ties to India; 'Indian American' for a U.S. permanent resident or citizen with Indian ancestry; do not confuse with 'American Indian' (indigenous peoples of the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose terms precisely to avoid conflating South Asian identities with Native American identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigenous — definition and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: No single official definition but UN criteria emphasize self-identification, historical continuity, links to territory and distinct cultures. In U.S. context tribal membership denotes Indigenous identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NAJA urges outlets to capitalize 'Indigenous' to avoid confusion with non-human indigenous uses. Avoid referring to Indigenous people as possessions of states (use 'Indigenous people of Wyoming' not 'Wyoming’s Indigenous people').

rubrics_metrics.name: indigenous religion — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to local and regional religious traditions shaped by language, kinship, mythologies and rituals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lumping indigenous religion under oversimplified labels; recognize uniqueness and local variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indo — modifier usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifier denoting Indian origin or India connection (e.g., Indo-U.S. relations); increasingly used to refer to South Asian diaspora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Indo-' consistently and clarify scope (India vs South Asia) to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indochina — geographic caution and connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, not necessarily Thailand and Burma (Myanmar). Term may have colonialist connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term cautiously and precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indonesian names — naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Indonesian names have two names; having only one name is also common; Muslim naming rules can be complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect local naming conventions and verify preferred name order when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: infantile paralysis — prefer 'polio'
rubrics_metrics.description: Infantile paralysis is an older term for poliomyelitis (polio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'polio' rather than 'infantile paralysis' and prefer phrasing such as 'He had polio as a child' over 'He suffers from polio.'

rubrics_metrics.name: injury/injuries — preferred verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to injuries as being 'sustained' or 'received,' not 'suffered,' unless the person prefers 'suffered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use person-preferred language and neutral verbs when reporting injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'inmate' — people-first alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'inmate' when referring to someone who is incarcerated; prefer people-centered constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'incarcerated people,' 'imprisoned people,' 'people in prison/jail,' or 'formerly incarcerated people.' Provide context such as facility name and sentence length when relevant; follow Marshall Project recommendations and include examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: inner city — avoid euphemism, prefer neutral terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Term often used as euphemism for lower-income districts and sometimes racialized neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral geographic descriptors (city center, downtown) and socioeconomic terms (under-resourced, low-income) instead of 'inner city.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane asylum/mental health hospital — preferred terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Old term 'insane asylum' is objectionable; prefer 'mental health hospital' or 'psychiatric hospital.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use medically accurate and non-stigmatizing facility names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane/insanity — avoid colloquial or offensive uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like insane, insanity and mentally deranged are offensive; the medical profession uses 'mental disorder' or 'mental illness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these terms except in quotes or where legally relevant (insanity defense). Use 'mental illness' or 'mental disorder' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: inscrutable — caution for racialized usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Although synonym for mysterious, 'inscrutable' is considered a racially charged adjective, especially when describing Asians or Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this adjective in racial/ethnic descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: institutional racism — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When policies and practices put non-dominant races at a disadvantage; reflected in housing, hiring, education, media and other systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that institutional racism can be structural rather than intentional. Use specific examples (school discipline as school-to-prison pipeline) and connect to systemic racism and White privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: intellectual disability — definition and person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability involving significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior, typically developing before age 18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use person-first language: 'a person with an intellectual disability' rather than 'intellectually disabled.' Cite authoritative definitions (American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: intelligent design — definition and reporting context
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that some aspects of life are too complex to arise without design and often associated with creationism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe intelligent design accurately and situate it within debates about evolution and creationism.

rubrics_metrics.name: interdenominational vs interfaith — distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdenominational: formally approved or under jurisdiction of more than one denomination. Interfaith: activities drawing people from entirely different religious traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the terms interchangeably; use 'ecumenical' for multiplicity of Christian traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: internment, Japanese — historical definition and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to WWII incarceration of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, two-thirds U.S. citizens, ordered to sell homes/businesses and move to relocation centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'internment' accurately and provide historical context (dates, consequences, releases in 1946) when reporting.
